meaningMnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means comfort .

See the two fists gripping the two vertical bars? They probably belong to a criminal , since criminals get put behind bars. It also looks like the bar on the left has been bent, like the criminal is trying to escape. Oh no…
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means festival .
A samurai opens his mouth to wish you good luck . Samurai are usually considered strong, silent types, but before any big battle they open their mouths to say one thing to each other: "good luck!"

This radical is made up of horns and older brother. Why horns? They're part of your older brother's new guard uniform. He's a guard now, of a bank or a museum. And the horns are actually part of his guard hat, which of course makes him a more intimidating guard.

Everyone used a slide ( 丿 ) to escape the many little cages ( 匚 ) you tried to boil ( 灬 ) them in, leaving you with nothing . Absolutely nothing inside those boiling cages. Which, to be honest, serves you right. Anyone who pulls a stunt like that deserves… nothing. Nothing at all.
The flowery paragraph isn't just regular writing. It's flowery, which makes it a poem .

This is the tiger radical. Try to imagine it as a tiger pouncing over a lowercase "t" — see its hind legs stretched out on the left, and its front paws reaching over the "t"? That "t" also stands for "tiger," obviously.

Should you let the sun shine on your coat rack ? Absolutely ! You should absolutely take advantage of the sun's natural freshening and deodorizing properties. Hints Pull a coat off your coat rack and give it a sniff. Don't you just love how fresh and sun-kissed it smells? You do. You absolutely do.
readingMnemonic: You're absolutely loving the effects of the sun on your coat rack — till a ze ppelin ( ぜ ) flies overhead and blocks it out. You absolutely need to get this zeppelin to move, ASAP. Hints You try leaving a stern note on the zeppelin's windshield: "You absolutely cannot hover your zeppelin here. I will call the authorities, and your zeppelin will absolutely be towed."

meaningMnemonic: You use a thread for good luck by bind ing two fingers together. You tie them nice and tight. Hints Tying two fingers together with a good luck thread is very common where you're from.
readingMnemonic: After you bind your fingers, the good luck starts pouring in. Literally. Suddenly ketsu p ( けつ ) starts pouring down from the heavens. Hints This ketsup is exactly what you were looking for, but now it won't stop. You need to get out of this bind by untying the thread on your finger. But it won't budge. It's covered in ketsup. Help! You're going to drown!

meaningMnemonic: Under a canopy your clan digs in the ground , trying to get to the bottom . They want to build a nice home your entire clan can live in, but they need to get to the bottom before they'll start building. Hints Picture all of the people in your clan under this canopy digging with all their might, trying to find the bottom. "Isn't there... no bottom though?" you think to yourself.
readingMnemonic: Suddenly someone down in the hole shouts that they've reached the bottom , but it's full of water and they're all soak ed ( そこ )! Hints The bottom is full of water, and everyone and everything down there is soaked through now.

meaningMnemonic: Your mouth is so big that it's the cause of all your problems. Hints Imagine all the dumb things you blabber about, with your mouth open big and wide. Saying things you shouldn't say, causing all kinds of drama. Shame on you.
readingMnemonic: Your big mouth is the cause behind all your friends and family moving to an inn ( いん ). They move to the inn so they don't have to live with you and hear you talk anymore. Hints Who knew you could cause people to live in an inn instead of their own homes with your big mouth...

meaningMnemonic: They say sheep are detailed creatures. I mean, I never thought sheep were very detailed, but that’s what they say. Hints Imagine getting really close to a sheep and seeing all the tiny detailed curls in their wool. There are hidden patterns you'd never noticed before now!
readingMnemonic: The reason these sheep are so detailed is that they are trying to impress the Shou gun ( しょう ). If they're fancy enough, perhaps the Shougun won’t kill them for their meat and make their wool into clothing. Hints Picture the Shougun, leaning in close to inspect the detailed patterns all over the sheep. His nose is so close, he can probably smell all the little detailed nuances of the sheep's musk too.

meaningMnemonic: If you can say what sound a drunkard makes, you must be very discerning . Few people are able to discern what sound a drunkard makes, but you — you can say, because you're a very discriminating listener. Hints Yes, you can even tell a tequila drunk from a vodka drunk based on the sounds they make. (Imagine how exactly they'd be different.) To be able to say what sound each kind of drunkard makes, it takes a very discerning, discriminating mind.
readingMnemonic: Discerning individuals like you are considered chic ( しき ). What's more chic than your discriminating way of listening? Hints All chic people show some kind of discernment. For some it's about discerning what's fashionable. For you, it's about discriminating one kind of drunk sound from another. That's your version of chic.

meaningMnemonic: A tiger kills a pig with a knife in this new drama about the animal kingdom! The tiger and pig used to be friends when they were younger, but now they're bitter enemies and the tiger just stabbed the pig right in the chest with a knife. Hints Picture this scene from the drama as dramatically as you can. The pig stares into the tiger's eyes, "Tiger, you wouldn't–uh!" The pig's eyes slowly lower to see the knife sticking into its gut, the tiger's hand still holding it. "This is what you get, you pig," the tiger spits back, twisting.
readingMnemonic: This drama is being put on by Gecki ( げき ), your childhood pet gecko. Gecki is playing all the parts, because as true drama fans know, one-gecko-shows are the highest form of art. Hints Picture Gecki acting out the part of the tiger and the pig in this drama. It's so intense, you're moved to tears. Bravo Gecki, bravo!

meaningMnemonic: The dry radical and the dry kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: You need to dry Genghis Khan ( かん ). He hates being wet, all of the Mongols do, so your job is to dry his entire body. And his clothes, and his horse. In fact, when it rains, you have to ride next to him keeping him dry by holding an umbrella above his head. Hints Imagine keeping Genghis Khan completely dry all day every day. He won't even get wet to bathe. Instead he makes you rub his body with dry sand and salts.

meaningMnemonic: A shellfish that can't live through winter is a failure . Any proper shellfish would survive through the winter, so this is quite an embarrassing defeat . Hints Imagine you're a shellfish in the cold, cold winter. The water is freezing but you must tough it out so no one will say you're a failure in spring when they find your dead, defeated shellfish body.
readingMnemonic: The best way to avoid failure is to say a little hai ku ( はい ) to distract you from the cold. In fact, this can work in any situation where you're afraid of defeat. Say a haiku aloud, it will calm your nerves and warm you from the inside. Hints Imagine being a shellfish freezing in the cold winter water, but you avoid failure by muttering haiku over and over to keep you warm and determined.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami is coming, and you want to walk over it, so you have to ford it. You don’t walk across a tsunami, you wade across it. Hints Imaging taking your shoes off, hiking up your pants, and holding all of your things above your head as you ford across the tsunami.
readingMnemonic: Your ability to ford this tsunami impresses everyone who witnesses it, especially the Shou gun ( しょう ). Now that you've taught him a tsunami can be forded, he's going to start sending his troops through them instead of waiting for them to pass. Hints Your new fording techniques have increased the Shougun's military power! Congrats, I guess.

meaningMnemonic: The fruit radical and the fruit kanji are exactly the same! Bodacious!
readingMnemonic: They sell fruit at the store, and you need to drive your ca r ( か ) to get there. A car is the fastest way to fruit. Hints Imagine you have a hankering for your favorite fruit. You gotta get in your car and put the pedal to the metal! Feel the wind in your hair as your car speeds down the road and listen to that engine purr.

meaningMnemonic: Under this roof is a bear who works for the government . If you saw a bear out in the wild you might be afraid and try to run, but if you see a bear inside a building under a roof, don't be scared! It's just a government bear. Hints Picture the government bear looking through government documents and snorting gruffly as it decides what to sign and what to reject. It has a little government sash and hat.
readingMnemonic: The first government that allowed bears was set up by Genghis Khan ( かん ). He was all about conquering people and then using them as efficiently as possible. He discovered that bears are incredibly useful in government buildings as government workers. Hints Picture Genghis Khan patting the first bear government worker on the back as they start their first day working for the government.

meaningMnemonic: Throw a net over someone so you can haul them into a government office and get their signature . Hints Whether it's a tax return or a marriage certificate, you need this person's signature on some official document, and you're going to drag them kicking and screaming into a government office to get it.
readingMnemonic: After everything wraps up at the government office and you get the person's signature , you take them out to see a show ( しょ ). Signing paperwork at a government office is never fun, but a nice show afterward makes it all worth it. Hints What kind of show are you going to take them to? Broadway? Cirque du Soleil? I'd go with something swanky to make up for the whole "kidnapping them with a net" thing.

meaningMnemonic: If you're on the roof of the festival you'll have to guess what's actually going on below you. You can kind of see that there are rides and maybe food? It smells like food. But you have to guess on the specifics because you're above it and not in it. Hints Imagine being on the roof above a festival. Can you guess what's happening below you based on the sounds and smells?
readingMnemonic: To get a better guess , you ask Satsu ki ( さつ ) for help. She's that little girl you know from some earlier mnemonics, and she happens to be up on the roof with you. Picture her as you ask, "What's your guess, Satsuki?" Hints And what's Satsuki doing up here, anyway? Your guess is as good as mine. Now imagine you and her trying to guess what kind of festival it is.

meaningMnemonic: A Viking will empty his mouth of all its dirt in the great hall . They all get together in some kind of public chamber and dish all the dirt (literal and figurative) that they've got. Hints Picture a long Viking hall, with a big table and tons of chairs. All of the Vikings are gossiping and sharing all their dirt on their enemies.
readingMnemonic: While the Vikings gather to spill the dirt in their hall , they also stuff their faces with dou ghnuts ( どう ). Ah yes, Vikings love to eat doughnuts when they talk trash. Hints Now picture all of the Vikings in the hall spitting dirt with one breath and shoveling doughnuts in with the next. It's pretty gross!

meaningMnemonic: You hide poop in a cape as part of the illusion in your magic show. Your acts are kind of gross and this one involves creating the illusion of disappearing poop by hiding it within the folds of your cape. Hints Imagine having poop in your cape. It would smell bad and anyone close to you would be able to smell right through the illusion.
readingMnemonic: Somehow the poop cape illusion goes over really well. The crowd is giving you a standing ovation and right in the center is Gen ji ( げん ). He marches up to you, wipes a tear from his eye, and says, "Your illusion cape is wonderful. I must have it!" Hints Genji grabs the cape before you can stop him and he puts it on. You can see the illusion fade, he keeps smiling but more tears start streaming down his face. "A wonderful illusion, the best I've ever seen," he chokes out and marches away, without looking back.

meaningMnemonic: A criminal has done an injustice on the world or other people. Being a criminal is a negative thing, and even if it was just a mistake , it was still a crime. Hints Think of all the criminals you know. Even if what they did was a mistake, it was still some type of injustice, right? It was something the rest of the world sees as a negative thing.
readingMnemonic: When you commit an injustice , you'll know because he at ( ひ ) fills your body. Maybe you've never done any kind of big thing, but when you make a mistake your face fills with heat and you turn red! Hints This is the heat of embarrassment, of knowing you did something negative or wrong.

meaningMnemonic: Put on cleat s so you can plant a kiss on your sweetheart's forehead in the heart of winter — that's love . You'll be braving the harsh winter elements for love, so you put on your cleats to get a better grip on the snow. Sure, you could just wait for better weather to go see them, but then it wouldn't be true love, would it? Hints Picture a person you love. Feel the joy of love in your heart as you brave the winter to see them. Your cleats crunch the snow underfoot, it's cold outside, but you're kept warm and happy by that feeling of love.
readingMnemonic: Walking through the winter snow with your cleats on, you've gotta keep your eye ( あい ) on the prize. It's a really hard journey, but you keep your eye on the prize, which is your love and the time you'll get to spend with them. Hints Imagine seeing your love with your own two eyes after a long time apart. It feels great to be reunited and see eye to eye once again. Imagine this feeling.

meaningMnemonic: Flowers can be used for comfort , but also for medicine . Sure, it’s a comfort to smell flowers because they smell nice, but one can also use them as medicine to heal people. Hints Imagine having some medicine that smells and tastes like fresh cut flowers. Smell the smell in your nose and taste the taste on your tongue.
readingMnemonic: The best way to transport all the medicine on land is with a yak ( やく ). Yaks are big, strong, and very capable of transporting flower medicine like these. Hints Picture a yak in your mind. Pretend you are riding atop the yak as it transports this medicine. Feel the fur of the yak in your hands as you cling on for dear life.

meaningMnemonic: Viking see , Viking memorize . That’s how Vikings learn things. They see something, and then they memorize it. Quite simple, really. It can also mean awake . Just remember that Vikings can't see if they aren't awake. There won't be anything to memorize if their eyes are still closed, after all! Hints How else would a Viking memorize something? Imagine having to memorize sea charts for your Viking navigation. Look and see the maps in your brain as you memorize them.
readingMnemonic: Every morning, a cock ( かく ) crows and rouses the Vikings. Seeing this, one of the Vikings memorize s the cock crow so that he can mimic it and play pranks on his fellow Vikings. Hints Imagine yourself memorizing the sound of a cock crow and using it to play jokes on your fellow Vikings. Cock-a-doodle-doo!

meaningMnemonic: A viking with a mouth towel is a totally normal thing. It's ordinary . Hints Vikings get a lot of nasty stuff on their mouths from their messy eating and pillaging, so it makes sense that they'd all have mouth towels. It's as ordinary and normal as it gets, at least amongst the vikings.
readingMnemonic: It's normal for a viking to have a mouth towel, but your sloppy farmhand friend Joe ( じょう ) has a mouth towel too. That's a habit that's only normal for vikings, so why does he have one? Hints When you ask Joe about his Viking mouth towel, he just tells you, "It's normal for everyone to have mouth towels. Totally ordinary." Now that you think about it, he really is a messy dude, so he probably needs it.

meaningMnemonic: You're all by your self and you have to check your rice paddie s — all twenty of them! Luckily, you have an incredible nose , so you can quickly assess the state of your twenty rice paddies with just a few sniffs. Hints Really focus in on your nose. Your nostrils get huge, and your nose is huge. Smell the rice and its freshness in your imagination. Your nose is amazing.
readingMnemonic: As you sniff your rice paddies, an unexpected smell wafts into your nose : 花 s ( はな ). Oh no — did you accidentally plant 花 s instead of rice? Oh well, the 花 s are putting your nose in such a state of bliss that you actually think things might be better this way. Hints Honestly, is there anything better to do with your nose than smell 花 s? 花 s and noses are a match made in heaven (unless you have pollen allergies…).

meaningMnemonic: The nothing radical and the nothing kanji are exactly the same! Woah!
readingMnemonic: Nothing can moo ( む ) quite like a cow can moo. Cows are the best at going moo. That’s a fact. Hints Listen to this cow moo. Can you do a better moo than this moo cow? Nope.

meaningMnemonic: The original radical and the original kanji are the same! This kanji can also mean field , probably because that's what everything originally looked like before humans: just a bunch of fields. Hints Know your radicals! I shouldn't even have to tell you this by now.
readingMnemonic: The original Japanese hero was Gen ji ( げん ), from "The Tale of Genji." Hints Picture Genji, the original Japanese protagonist, walking through the streets. He's signing his name for swooning ladies and gentlemen. Genji is the OG (original Genji).

meaningMnemonic: If there is a drum in your mouth it's time to rejoice ! And because of your mouth drum your rejoicing will be loud and booming! Hints Imagine having a drum in your mouth and rejoicing about it! Imagine how loud it would be!
readingMnemonic: You loudly rejoice for a while when suddenly someone runs over and shoves a key ( き ) in your mouth, locking it shut. You can't rejoice anymore! You need that key to unlock your mouth! Hints Imagine if people could just stop the rejoicing of others by locking their mouths shut with keys. What a sad world.

meaningMnemonic: Again and again, your heart comes back to the same person. Is this romance ? Are you in love ? Hints Perhaps you have a person in mind that your heart comes back to again and again. Associate that person with this notion and kanji, and this'll be easy to memorize!
readingMnemonic: But, remember that your romance isn’t a ren tal ( れん ). You really wanna reserve it for the right person! Hints Don’t let your love become a rental. Wait for the right person to come around.

meaningMnemonic: A criminal 's heart will always be sad . No one chooses a life of crime if they're happy. And even if they seem like they're doing fine on the outside, deep down they're really sad. Hints Imagine watching a criminal after he's done stealing from a bank. He's all alone. He stops throwing the money around. And cries. So so sad.
readingMnemonic: The sad feelings fill the criminal's body with he at ( ひ ). This heat spreads and radiates out. If you walk next to them on the street, you'll feel the sad heat floating by you. Hints Imagine being so sad that your entire body fills with heat. That heat even makes squiggly heat lines pop out above and around you.

meaningMnemonic: In the dirt , there's a gun . Its mouth points toward a plate . What's on the plate? Why, it's salt ! Hints In olden days, salt was so valuable it was used as money. So imagine the gun buried in the dirt, its mouth vigilantly guarding the plate of salt.
readingMnemonic: When you see the salt , you think to yourself, " She owe s ( しお ) me big time, so I'm going to go ahead and snatch her salt!" Who is she, you ask? She's the lady who owns the salt. And the gun in the dirt, of course. Hints Are you sure you want to take her salt? Sure, she owes you, but I don't think you want to argue with the mouth of a gun.

meaningMnemonic: In a yurt you use a towel as a seat . Hints Picture this yurt, with towels laid out as seats for everyone who visits.
readingMnemonic: Something about using a towel for a seat is very sexy ( せき ) to you. Probably because you associate it with sexy people using towel seats on the beach. Hints Imagine the sexiest person you've ever seen, using a towel as a seat next to you in this yurt. Maybe they're in a bathing suit. Maybe they're completely covered up. Either way, they're very sexy.

meaningMnemonic: The leader of the shellfish has a knife in his side . It's fine though, don't worry — if anything, it makes him look more battle-hardened and leader-like. Hints Picture the shellfish leader in your mind and make sure to pay special attention to the knife that's sticking out of his side. It's right in the groove of his shell.
readingMnemonic: Who stuck this knife in the shellfish leader's side ? Sir Gawa in ( がわ ), knight of the Round Table. He mistook him for the Green Knight and stabbed him in the side before realizing his mistake. Hints Imagine the horror on Sir Gawain's face when he realized he had knifed the wrong guy in the side. "Wow, I am so sorry. From a distance, your shell looked kind of green and armor-y, but… I really didn't do my due diligence on this one. Is your side okay?"

meaningMnemonic: When you swing your axe , the ground ends up covered in fins , because you're a soldier . Only a skilled axe soldier could make such precise cuts as to de-fin a bunch of fish like that. Hints Imagine trying to carve some fish with an axe, to get them ready to eat. Not an easy thing to do. If you're a trained axe soldier, it'll probably be a lot easier. So picture yourself chopping off fins as an expert axe soldier.
readingMnemonic: Uh-oh, it looks like this axe soldier was so excited about chopping the fins off his fish that he didn't think about how he was going to cook them. The only thing nearby to light on fire is a bale of hay ( へい ). Well, it's not the best thing, but at least it will get these fish cooked. Hints Imagine this soldier lighting a bale of hay on fire to cook his fish. The hay burns really fast, but it should be enough.

meaningMnemonic: What do you say to a guard ? Your theory about how the thing he's guarding isn't even real. Yeah, you have this whole thing figured out. You have for a while. At this point, it's only fair that you tell your theory to the guard who's wasting his time. Hints Imagine saying your theory out loud to a guard about how what he's guarding isn't even there. Imagine how he would react.
readingMnemonic: The guard listens to your theory but then he says his OWN! He thinks there are two sets ( せつ ) of guarded items, and he's only guarding one. According to his theory, either one could be real! His theory is more plausible, don't you think? Hints Which theory do you believe? That there is nothing or that there are sets of things?

meaningMnemonic: If you take a thread and plant a rice paddy on it, the rice paddy is going to be extremely thin , but also detailed . Hints Imagine this thin thread of rice paddy. It looks so detailed because all the rice paddy stuff is contained in this thin thread shape. You could maybe get one narrow line of rice on this thing.
readingMnemonic: This thin rice paddy is for your cy borg ( さい ). You gave your cyborg a very thin human stomach, so it can only digest one thin line of rice at a time. Hints Picture the cyborg eating a really thin piece of rice. Now it's completely full! What a smart, thrifty cyborg.

meaningMnemonic: The tree you aim your gun at from your window is an ume tree, aka a Japanese plum tree. Why? Because shooting the ume out of Japanese plum trees is, in your opinion, the best way to harvest them. Hints Imagine picking fruit off an ume tree this way, shooting it off the branches with your gun. You take aim at an unsuspecting ume — BANG! The gunshot rings in your ears and the smell of gunpowder fills the air. The ume branch is now one ume lighter.
readingMnemonic: You've probably heard of ume before, depending on your exposure to Japan. Since the word itself is Japanese, the reading is also うめ . Hints Imagine eating your harvest of ume. Taste the sour, astringent flesh of these Japanese plums as you stuff your gluttonous face. Then, feel a stomach ache start to come on… Maybe this is why people normally pickle these before eating them.

meaningMnemonic: You have a poem about winter that you say to warn people against going outside. It's cold and dangerous in winter! You admonish anyone and everyone you see going out there with your scary winter poem. Hints Imagine the things you'd warn people about. What is it about winter that's so dangerous?
readingMnemonic: To make sure people listen to your warn ing, you threaten to take away their ca ke ( けい ). People will do anything for cake, so when you bring it up, they actually take your attempts to warn them about winter seriously. Hints The winter cold will make you ache Your whole body will start to shake Don't go outside I'll eat your cake

meaningMnemonic: When a seat is lack ing the person it's supposed to have in it, there is an absence . Where is Johnny? Another absence? Ugh. Johnny. C'mon.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note that the けつ is shortened to けっ as つ s often are when in a situation like this.

meaningMnemonic: Absolutely an injustice ! We must absolutely punish the perpetrator, by all means . First, though, we should probably define right and wrong . This word means "absolutely" when it's used as an adverb, and that's the use you'll hear most in conversation. However, as a noun it means "right and wrong", as in whether something is right or wrong, or good or bad.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: Please let me hear your opinion by all means.

meaningMnemonic: The Love Know Prefecture ! I want to live here, because people must know love! Of course, we don't call it that in English. You'll have to know the reading of the kanji to know the reading of this prefecture, which is Aichi Prefecture (jump to the reading to figure this out).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn 知 's on'yomi when you learned the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You know what they really love to know about in Aichi Prefecture ? Chee se ( ち ). Those folks in Aichi, they're some real cheese know-it-alls. Don't ever bring one to a wine and cheese party, because, man — they will be rattling off cheese facts to you all evening.

meaningMnemonic: The particle に here is a clue that this word is an adverb. An adverb describes actions, so what's a normal action? It's one you're always , or constantly , doing. That's what makes it normal!
readingMnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn. In order to learn it, think of this: I always tune ( つね ) my violin, but today I didn't tune it. So, now I sound terrible. Imagine how terrible my untuned violin sounds, compared to how it always sounds.

sentences.english: It takes some kids a while to realize their parents aren’t always right.

meaningMnemonic: Someone with " nothing " for their name is either trying to remain anonymous or is simply unknown .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: フグは、無名のまま死にたくないと思っている。
sentences.english: Fugu doesn’t want to die in anonymity.

meaningMnemonic: You learned that 付き合う means "to keep company with," and this is its noun version. When you keep company with someone, you have an association or a relationship with them. 付き合い refers to ongoing interactions or connections with people, like 人付き合い (social relationships) or 長い付き合い (a longstanding association). It can also refer to the obligations that result from such relationships, like 付き合いで飲みに行く (go drinking out of social obligation). You may not want to go, but… society demands it. You'll also sometimes see it with the honorific お , as in お付き合い — especially when referring to business associations or respectfully talking about romantic relationships.

sentences.english: She made a wish on the first star.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: I went to see a movie on Christmas day in the U.S. and I was surprised to see that the theater was nearly empty.

meaningMnemonic: A song drama . Ugh, I hate these. They sing so much and they're so dramatic. This is an opera . 歌劇 is a formal word for opera that is typically used in theatrical or artistic contexts. In everyday speech, people usually just say オペラ .

sentences.english: I became a fan of a French actor in one of the operas.

meaningMnemonic: The original thing you make is the original work . It's always better to have the original, rather than a copy, I think.

sentences.english: I got an autograph from the original author.

meaningMnemonic: The outside side is the outside .

meaningMnemonic: When you have love for your country deep within your heart , that is patriotism .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: Since you live in Japan, it is natural to have patriotism toward Japan.

sentences.japanese: 愛国心がやたらに強い男が、トーフグに入社しました。
sentences.english: A very patriotic man joined Tofugu.

meaningMnemonic: They warn you and they guess when you've done something wrong (with evidence, of course!). They are the police .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 動くな！警察だ。
sentences.english: Don't move! It's the police.

sentences.japanese: 警察に電話した方がいいんじゃない？
sentences.english: Maybe we should call the police?

meaningMnemonic: When your power is nothing you are powerless .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. There are a couple possibilities for 力 though, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember which to use: You know 力 uses its りょく reading here because you're totally powerless when they lock ( りょく ) you up. Who's "they"? I don't know, but did you hear the click of the lock behind you? That means you're powerless now.

sentences.japanese: 親は無力ですよ。子が大きくなると、してあげられることなんて、ほとんどありません。
sentences.english: Parents are helpless. When a child grows up, there is very little you can do for them.

sentences.japanese: 自分の無力さを知り、情けない気持ちでいっぱいになりました。

sentences.japanese: できないことが多すぎて無力感がハンパないですが、とにかく今日できることをやっていきます。
sentences.english: There are too many things I can't do, and I feel incredibly powerless, but I'll do what I can today, no matter what.

meaningMnemonic: The right side is the right side .

meaningMnemonic: A nothing occurrence is an occurrence where nothing happens to you, or at least nothing too bad — that means you're safe and sound . Phew! In addition to meaning safe , 無事 can also describe a situation where everything goes off without a hitch .
readingMnemonic: One thing that's not safe and sound is the reading of the 無 in this word. Instead of む it's ぶ . Why? Because you thought it was safe and sound, but you were fooled. There are ghosts everywhere, all jumping out and screaming Boo! ( ぶ ) at you. Feel the surprise. You thought it was safe and sound!

meaningMnemonic: You've learned the word 塩 , meaning salt. Add コショウ , which means pepper, and you get salt and pepper . You haven't learned the word for pepper yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: If salt wanted to start a cooking podcast, who would be a better co-show ( コショウ ) host than pepper? Imagine the most classic pair of seasonings getting into a studio to co-show host a podcast. Now that's a spicy combo. Just a side note: The コショウ part can also be written in different ways, such as in kanji, all hiragana, or as コショー , especially on product packaging.
readingMnemonic: 塩 uses the same reading you learned with the vocabulary, and if you remember your katakana too, you should be able to read this.

sentences.english: My mom puts salt and pepper in her pudding.

meaningMnemonic: This is a day of the week. You know this because it has 曜日 in it. But what day of the week is it? The dirt day is the day you finally get to go outside and get a little dirty. Maybe you're in the yard gardening, at the park playing baseball, or even riding dirt bikes somewhere with buddies. Or maybe you're just lying face down in the dirt 'cause you drank too much on Friday. Either way, Saturday is the day for getting down and dirty.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just watch out for the ひ becoming a び like it did in the word 曜日 .

meaningMnemonic: If you love your self that is self love . You’ll mostly see this word as part of the set phrase ご自愛下さい , which is used in emails and the like to remind the recipients to be good to themselves. Other variations include ご自愛くださいませ , ご自愛を , and ご自愛のほどを .
readingMnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji, you self lover you.

meaningMnemonic: If you're like everyone else learning a new language, you learn the bad words first. This isn't a bad word, but it sort of contains one. くそ means "sh*t" (as in "poop") in Japanese. What is your nose sh*t, then? It's your snot and boogers . Eww, stop eating them!

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of thin ? It also appears in expressions where something is figuratively "thin," like 食が細い (having a small appetite) and 声が細い (having a faint voice).

meaningMnemonic: You've seen how 変える means "to change" something. This word means that something changed by itself, so it means to be changed or to be altered . 変わる refers to the act of changing into something different, and involves alterations in nature, appearance, or state. For example, it can describe changes in weather or the season, someone undergoing a noticeable change in appearance or behavior, or one's feelings or thoughts evolving over time. Since 変わる means "becoming something different," you can also use 変わった and 変わっている to describe someone or something that's "different from what's normal." For example, you can say 変わった人 or 変わっている人 to mean "an odd person."
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means defeat , so this means to be defeated , but also to be unsuccessful .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have been defeated. You lay there on the ground, and the fans around the stadium are disgusted with your performance. Some hipster walks up to you and says: " Yah, Boo " ( やぶ ) referring to how poorly you did. "No boo!", you reply back. "Yah boo", they say again.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means sad and this verb is transitive, so it means to be sad about something. Boohoo.
readingMnemonic: If you're going to be sad about something right now, it will be kana ( かな ). Don't use kana when you're trying to learn kanji! You'll be sad forever if you're stuck using kana your whole life, so don't let that habit start now, friend.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means cure , so this verb means to cure , to heal or to ease something. This verb is for when someone actively cures something. (The illness doesn't just get better on its own.) How can you remember that? Because when you try to cure someone and you mess up, they can sue ( す ). Basically, to cure someone is to risk getting sued.
readingMnemonic: This word uses a kun'yomi reading you didn't learn with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic: I need you to cure him, and I need you to cure him right now ( なお ). NOW NOW NOW! This also shares a reading with 直す , a similar word that you already learned means "to fix." Fixing and curing are basically the same, right? Call me crazy, but there might just be an etymological connection there that can help you remember this reading.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means guess so the verb vocab version is to guess . Alternatively, you can learn this as to sense or to presume .

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same, so this means ume . Despite sometimes being called a " Japanese plum " or a " Japanese apricot ," an ume is its own distinct fruit, and it's nothing like the plums or apricots you're probably used to eating. Ume are super sour and not particularly fun to eat raw, so they're usually either eaten pickled or used to make Japanese plum wine.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. It's also the same as the meaning of the kanji / vocab, though you can think of this as Japanese plum as well if you want.
